en: # Data written on Monday, 7 April 2025 at 13:49:25.
definition: Word: Mean Absolute Error (ignored, the filename is the actual word) Plural: 0 Definition: A type of distance metric which is a variation of the Manhattan metric. It includes a normalisation step which divides the Manhattan distance by the number of dimensions involved, giving $\\text{MAE} = \\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\left| a_i - b_i \\right|$. MAE is used primarily in statistics to compare data sets, for example by testing the accuracy of predictions against a collection of measurements. It also makes it possible to compare distances measured in spaces with different number of dimensions. MAE employs symmetric penalisation, in that accuracy improvements and worsenings of identical magnitude cancel each other out, resulting in identical accuracy evaluations. en: # Data written on Thursday, April 22, 2021 at 14:06:23.
definition: Word: Gaussian (ignored, the filename is the actual word) Plural: 0 Definition: A type of colour interpolation used in colour gradients. The colour of any given gradient location is a combination of all grip colours, weighted by the distance to each grip. The closer the grip, the more effect its colour has. This effect diminishes as the distance from the grip increases, following the Gaussian bell curve. The weight of a grip at distance $d$ is $w = e^{-\\left(\\frac{d}{r}\\right)^2}$. Unlike all other interpolations, Gaussian does not guarantee that the colour of the gradient *at* a specific grip is indeed the colour of that grip. The colour grips are treated as suggestions rather than constraints.  The benefit of a Gaussian gradient is that it is the only interpolation which is always continuous under grip location changes. That is, a small change to the position of one grip always yields a small change to the total gradient, even if the small change affects the sort order of the grips. IPA: 'ɡaʊsɪən Internal:  External:  Author: Robert McNeel & Associates Notes:  AutoLink: True State: Finished

Unlike with other hue-saturation spaces, the `H*` axis is adjusted by a non-linear squeezing and stretching transformation to increase the respective areas associated with yellow, cyan and magenta hues, which tend to be underrepresented in the HSV and HSL spaces. en: Word: Root Mean Squared Error (ignored, the filename is the actual word)

RMSE is much more sensitive to large errors than the Mean Absolute Error, as all errors are squared prior to computing the average. en: Word: Span (ignored, the filename is the actual word)
definition: Plural:  Class: Noun Definition: A subdomain of a NURBS curve or surface bounded by two consecutive knots. A span represents a portion of a NURBS shape which can be described using a single polynomial equation. Piecewise geometries operate on the basis of joining small, easily described pieces into a more complex whole. In the case of NURBS, the pieces are usually called spans. There is a minor distinction to be made when the NURBS curve contains multiple knots; while these give rise to zero-length spans, there is no such thing as a zero-length piece. en: Word: Very Large Number (ignored, the filename is the actual word)

This is the reason why far-from-origin geometry ought to be avoided, and why calculations with very large decimal numbers should be considered suspect. en: Word: Zipf Distribution (ignored, the filename is the actual word)
definition: Plural: 0 Class: Noun Definition: A type of discrete distribution describing the ubiquity and rarity of values in a data set. E.g. the frequency of words in a language form a Zipf distribution, with a few words such as "the" and "you" occurring very frequently, a somewhat larger group of words which occur fairly regularly such as "chair" and "watch", but with the majority of words being very rare, such as "sonorous" or "latibule". The frequency of the $k$-th most common value follows\: $$f(k) \\propto \\frac{1}{k^s}$$  This distribution is related to the continuous Pareto Distribution, both being governed by power law decay. However, there are significant differences, such as the limited domain of Zipf versus the infinite range of Pareto. Notation\: `Zipf(exponent\:1.0, n\:100)` ![Zipf Distribution](pdf=zipf) IPA: zɪpf dɪstrɪˈbjuːʃ(ə)n Internal:  External:  Author: Robert McNeel & Associates Notes:  AutoLink: True State: Finished
